profile.name: Polska
profile.tagline: Sweden's national turning dance and a shared Nordic partner tradition.
profile.insight: Rooted in 17th-century Polish court visits, the polska evolved into a dizzying Nordic partner dance where couples rotate once every single measure.
profile.profile: The polska is a family of music and dance forms shared across the Nordic countries, including Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and Estonia. Tracing its roots back to 17th-century court influences, it combines asymmetric rhythms, soaring fiddle melodies, and high-speed couple turns. While Norway maintains a vibrant living tradition, Swedish polska choreography was largely reconstructed from mid-20th-century field research. Today, it stands as a cornerstone of Nordic traditional folk culture.
profile.profile_long:
The polska (Swedish plural polskor) represents a vast and diverse family of music and dance forms spread across the Nordic region, appearing as polsk in Denmark, polka or polska in Estonia, and under numerous local designations in Norway such as pols, springleik, and springar. The origins of the form are frequently connected to the cultural influence of the Polish court during the early 17th century, though some scholars trace elements back to earlier indigenous Nordic songs and triple-meter melodies that blended with incoming continental styles like the polonaise and minuet.

In Norway, the tradition remains strikingly alive in mountain regions and rural communities. Norwegian variants include the rhythmic pols of eastern valleys—characterized by promenades, counter-clockwise bakmes turns, and rapid clockwise pols turns—and the springar of western fjords, danced to the haunting, droning notes of the Hardanger fiddle (hardingfele). In Sweden, while instrumental fiddle traditions passed unbroken through generations, the actual dancing suffered heavily during 20th-century industrialization. Consequently, modern knowledge of Swedish polska largely derives from meticulous field research conducted in the 1940s, 50s, and 60s, capturing hundreds of regional variations across provinces like Dalarna and Småland.

Musically and choreographically, polskas are generally categorized by rhythm style: sixteenth-note (semiquaver) polskas featuring smooth, even phrasing; eighth-note (quaver) polskas with distinctive asymmetrical beats where fiddlers tap only the first and third beats; and triplet polskas common in western borderlands. Couples navigate the dance floor through a continuous interplay of close-position rotation, open escort walking steps, and intricate underarm turns, making the polska a physically demanding and expressive partner tradition.

sections.origins_and_history: The roots of the polska are traced to 17th-century Polish court influences interacting with indigenous Nordic musical structures and older triple-meter folk songs.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced primarily as a couple, featuring walking promenades, counter-clockwise upper-body turns (bakmes), and rapid clockwise rotations (pols) executed in triple time.
sections.music_and_instruments: Played on standard violins and the Hardanger fiddle, structured around repeating 32 or 64-measure phrases with variable rhythmic accents.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditionally performed in regional Nordic folk costumes within community halls, village squares, and mountain settlements.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed socially at community gatherings, weddings, and festivals across Sweden, Norway, and neighboring Nordic regions.
sections.notable_figures: Archivists and researchers such as those from Svenskt visarkiv and regional contributors who documented disappearing traditions in the mid-20th century.
sections.regional_variants: Includes Norwegian pols and springar, Swedish slängpolskas in Småland, and diverse community styles across Dalarna and Uppland.
sections.lineage: Descended from 17th-century European court dances and Nordic folk songs; gave rise to modern forms like the Swedish hambo.

basic_steps: Resting step on beats one and three
teaching.rhythm: Triple time (3/4) with variable beat weights and asymmetrical phrasing
teaching.formation: Partner dance moving counter-clockwise around the room or on a fixed spot
teaching.level_notes: Requires strong core stability, balance, and coordination for rapid rotational steps.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Semiquaver, quaver, or triplet groupings with lengthened second beats in specific regional styles
music_profile.musical_form: Two or three eight-bar phrases, each repeated (32 to 64 measures per tune cycle)
music_profile.sound_description: Fiddles drive the melody through repeating motifs, drone strings on the Hardanger fiddle, and uneven beats where musicians traditionally tap only the first and third beats.

movement_profile.posture: Upper body facing as a couple, maintaining a close embrace or escort position
movement_profile.footwork: Walking promenade steps, stepping primarily on the first and third beat during resting phases
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: close hold escort position underarm turns
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Rotating counter-clockwise in bakmes and clockwise in pols rotations
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Couples traveling counter-clockwise around the periphery of the floor or stationary on a spot
movement_profile.partnering: Partner dance led by the male through a sequence of holds, turns, and promenades
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Fast, driving triple meter with organic pulse shifts

signature_moves.name: Bakmes turn
signature_moves.description: Counter-clockwise couple rotation at a rate of one revolution per two measures

signature_moves.name: Pols turn
signature_moves.description: Clockwise couple rotation at a rate of one full turn per measure

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Grounded footwork with rapid rotation; no major aerial jumps documented
